bio.en: Edwin Chen is the founder and CEO of Surge AI, the leading AI data company that powers training at every frontier AI lab and became the fastest company ever to reach $1 billion in revenue—bootstrapped, with under 100 people, and profitable from day one.
bio.zh: Edwin Chen 是 Surge AI 的创始人兼 CEO；Surge AI 是领先的 AI 数据公司，为每一家前沿 AI 实验室的训练提供支撑，并以最快速度在四年内依靠不到 100 人、零融资、自第一天起盈利的模式跻身十亿美元营收俱乐部。

summary.en: Edwin explains why data quality—not just model architecture—is the real bottleneck in building great AI, and how Surge trains models on what 'good' actually means with a tiny, elite, bootstrapped team. He argues many labs are optimizing for engagement and 'AI slop' rather than truth and human progress, and warns against a Silicon Valley game that mistakes throwing bodies at problems for real capability. The conversation also covers how to choose the right model behavior, why values shape models, and what it takes to build an important company differently.
summary.zh: Edwin 阐释了为何数据质量（而非仅仅是模型架构）才是打造优秀 AI 的真正瓶颈，以及 Surge 如何用一支精悍、精英化、自筹资金的小团队来训练模型理解何为“好”。他认为许多实验室在优化“engagement”和“AI 垃圾内容”而非真相与人类进步，并警示那种以为“堆人”就能提升能力的硅谷游戏。对话还涉及如何选择正确的模型行为、价值观如何塑造模型，以及以不同方式打造一家重要公司需要什么。

Yeah, you say it's a great problem. But that's completely different from what we want. We are looking for a Nobel Prize-winning poetry. Is this poetry unique? Is it full of subtle imagery? Does it surprise you and target your heart? Does it teach you something about the nature of moonlight? Does it playthrough emotions? And does it make you think? That's what we are thinking about when we think about high quality poem. (00:10:34): So it might be like a haiku about moonlight on water. It might use internal rhyme and meter. There are a thousand ways to write a poem about the moon, and in each one, gives you all these different insights into language, and imagery, and human expression, and I think thinking about quality in this way is really hard, it's hard to measure. It's really subjective, and complex, and rich. And it sets a really high bar. And so we have to build all of this technology in order to measure it, like thousands of signals on all of our workers, thousands of signals on every project, every task. We know at the end of the day, if you are good at writing poetry versus good at writing essays versus great at writing technical documentation. And so we have to gather all these signals on what your background is, what your expertise is, and not just that. Like how you're actually performing when you're writing all these things, and we use those signals to inform whether or not you are good [inaudible 00:11:23] for these projects, and whether or not you are improving the models. (00:11:26): And it's really hard, and so to build all this technology to measure it, but I think that's exactly what we want AI to do, and so we have these really deep notions about quality that we're always trying to try and achieve.
turns.zh: 我认为大多数人都不明白质量在这个领域意味着什么。他们认为你可以通过投入大量精力来解决问题并获得良好的数据，但这是完全错误的。让我举个例子。 (00:09:59)：假设您想要训练一个模型来写一首关于月亮的八行诗。是什么使它成为一首优秀的、高质量的诗？如果你不深入思考质量，你会说，“这是一首诗吗？它有八行吗？它包含月亮这个词吗？”您检查所有这些框，如果是的话，当然可以。是的，你说这是一个大问题。但这与我们想要的完全不同。我们正在寻找诺贝尔奖获得者的诗歌。这首诗有独特之处吗？是不是充满了微妙的意象？它是否让你感到惊讶并瞄准你的心？它能让你了解月光的本质吗？它会通过情感来发挥作用吗？这会让你思考吗？当我们思考高质量的诗歌时，这就是我们所思考的。 (00:10:34)：所以这可能就像一首关于水上月光的俳句。它可能会使用内部韵律和韵律。写一首关于月亮的诗有一千种方法，每一种都可以给你对语言、意象和人类表达的不同见解，我认为以这种方式思考质量真的很困难，很难衡量。它确实是主观的、复杂的、丰富的。它设定了一个非常高的标准。因此，我们必须构建所有这些技术来对其进行测量，例如我们所有工人的数千个信号，每个项目、每项任务的数千个信号。归根结底，我们知道您是否擅长写诗、擅长写论文还是擅长撰写技术文档。因此，我们必须收集所有这些信号，了解您的背景、专业知识，而不仅仅是这些。就像您在编写所有这些内容时的实际表现一样，我们使用这些信号来判断您是否适合这些项目[听不清 00:11:23]，以及您是否正在改进模型。 (00:11:26)：这真的很困难，所以建立所有这些技术来测量它，但我认为这正是我们希望人工智能做的事情，所以我们对质量有这些非常深刻的概念，我们一直在努力尝试和实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is there's kind of just going much deeper in understanding what quality is within the verticals that you are selling data around. And is this like a person you hire that is incredibly talented at poetry plus evals that they, I guess, help write, that tell them that this is great? What's the mechanics of that?
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是，需要更深入地了解您所销售数据的垂直领域的质量。这是否就像你雇用的一个在诗歌方面非常有天赋的人，我想他们会帮助撰写评估，告诉他们这很棒？其中的机制是什么？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: The way it works is we essentially gather thousands of signals about everything that you're doing when you're working on platform. So we are looking at your keyboard strokes. We are looking how fast you answer things. We are using reviews, we are using code standards, we are using... We're training models ourselves all on the outputs that you create, and then we're seeing whether they improve the model's performance. (00:12:23): And so in a very similar way to how Google search, like when Google search is trying to determine what is a good webpage, there's almost two aspects of it. One is you want to remove all of the worst of the worst webpages. So you want to remove all the spam, all the just low quality content, all the pages that don't load, and so it's almost like a content moderation problem. You just want to remove the worst of the worst. (00:12:44): But then you also want to discover the best of the best. Okay, like this is the best webpage or just the best person for this job. They are not just somebody who writes the equivalent of high school level poetry. Again, they're not just [inaudible 00:12:57] writing poetry that checks all these boxes, checks all of these explicit instructions, but rather, yeah, they're writing poetry that makes you emotional. And so we have all these signals as well that, again, completely differently from moving the worst of the worst, we are finding the best of the best. And so we have all these signals... (00:13:12): Again, just like Google Search uses all these signals that feeds them into their ML algorithms and uses and predicts certain types of things, we do the same with all of our workers and all of our tasks in all of our projects. And so it's almost like a complicated machine learning problem at the end of the day, and that's how it works.
turns.zh: 它的工作方式是，我们本质上收集了数千个关于您在平台上工作时所做的一切的信号。所以我们正在查看您的键盘敲击。我们正在观察您回答问题的速度。我们正在使用评论，我们正在使用代码标准，我们正在使用......我们正在根据您创建的输出自行训练模型，然后我们看看它们是否可以提高模型的性能。 (00:12:23)：与谷歌搜索的方式非常相似，就像谷歌搜索试图确定什么是一个好的网页一样，它几乎有两个方面。一是您想删除所有最糟糕的网页。因此，您想要删除所有垃圾邮件、所有低质量内容、所有无法加载的页面，因此这几乎就像内容审核问题。你只想消除最坏的情况中的最坏的情况。 (00:12:44)：但是您也想发现最好的。好吧，就像这是最好的网页或者只是最适合这项工作的人。他们不仅仅是写出相当于高中水平诗歌的人。再说一次，他们不只是[听不清 00:12:57] 写诗歌来检查所有这些方框，检查所有这些明确的指示，而是，是的，他们写的诗歌让你情绪化。因此，我们也有所有这些信号，再次表明，与移动最坏的最坏的情况完全不同，我们正在寻找最好的。所以我们有所有这些信号... (00:13:12)：同样，就像 Google 搜索使用所有这些信号将它们输入到 ML 算法中并使用和预测某些类型的事物一样，我们对所有项目中的所有工作人员和所有任务也执行相同的操作。所以归根结底，这几乎就像一个复杂的机器学习问题，这就是它的工作原理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is incredibly interesting. (00:13:31): I want to ask you about something I've been very curious about over the past couple years. If you look at Claude, it's been so much better at coding and at writing than any other model for so long. And it's really surprising just how long it took other companies to catch up. Considering just how much economic value there is there, just like every AI coding product sat on top of Claude because it was so good Claude code and writing also. What is it that made it so much better? Is it just the quality of the data they trained on or is there something else?
turns.zh: 这非常有趣。 (00:13:31)：我想问你一些我在过去几年里一直很好奇的事情。如果你看看 Claude，你会发现长期以来，他在编码和写作方面比任何其他模型都要好得多。令人惊讶的是其他公司花了多长时间才赶上来。考虑到那里有多少经济价值，就像每个人工智能编码产品都坐在克劳德之上一样，因为它是非常好的克劳德代码和写作。是什么让它变得如此好？这仅仅是他们训练的数据的质量还是还有其他原因？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I think there are multiple parts to it. So a big part of it certainly is the data. I think people don't realize that there's almost like this infinite amount of choices that all the frontier labs are deciding between when they're choosing what data goes into their models. It's like, okay, are you purely using human data? Are you gathering the human data in X, Y, Z way? When you are gathering the human data, what exactly are you asking the people who are creating it to create for you? (00:14:30): For example, in the coding realm, maybe you care more about front end coding versus back end coding. Maybe when you're doing front end coding, you care a lot about the visual design of the front end applications that you're creating, or maybe you don't care about it so much and you care more about, I don't know, the deficiency of it or the pure correctness over that visual design. (00:14:47): And then other questions like, okay, are you carrying [inaudible 00:14:49] how much synthetic data are we throwing into the mix? How much do you care about these 20 different benchmarks?" (00:14:55): Some companies, they see these benchmarks and they're like, "Okay, for PR purposes, even though we don't think that these academic benchmarks matter all that much, maybe we just need to optimize for them anyways because our marketing team needs to show certain progress on certain standard evaluations that every other company talks about, and if we don't show good performance here, it's going to be bad for us even if ignoring these academic benchmarks makes us better at the real tasks." (00:15:21): Other companies are going to be principled and be like, "Okay, yeah, no, I don't care about marketing. I just care about how my model performs on these real world tasks at the end of the day, and so I'm going to optimize for that instead." (00:15:31): And it's almost like there's a trade-off between all of these different things, and there's like a... (00:15:36): One of the things I often think about is that there's a... It's almost like there's an art to post training. It's not purely a science. When you are deciding what kind of model you're trying to create and what it's good at, there's this notion of taste and sophistication, like, "Okay, do I think that these..." (00:15:57): So going back to the example of how good the model is at visual design. I'm like, "Okay, maybe you have a different notion of visual design than what I do. Maybe you care more about minimalism, and you care more about, I don't know, 3D animations than I do. And maybe this other person prefers things that look a little bit more broke." And there's all these notions of taste sophistication that you have to decide between when you're designing your post training mix, and so that matters as well. (00:16:21): So long story short, I think there's all these different factors, and certainly the data is a big part of it, but it's also like what is the objective function that you're trying to optimize your model towards?
turns.zh: 我认为它有多个部分。所以其中很大一部分肯定是数据。我认为人们没有意识到，所有前沿实验室在选择将哪些数据放入模型时都需要在无数种选择之间做出选择。就像，好吧，你纯粹使用人类数据吗？您是否以 X、Y、Z 方式收集人类数据？当您收集人类数据时，您到底要求创建数据的人为您创建什么？ (00:14:30)：例如，在编码领域，也许您更关心前端编码而不是后端编码。也许当你进行前端编码时，你非常关心你正在创建的前端应用程序的视觉设计，或者也许你不太关心它，你更关心，我不知道，它的缺陷或视觉设计的纯粹正确性。 (00:14:47)：然后还有其他问题，比如，好吧，你携带[听不清 00:14:49] 我们要投入多少合成数据？你对这 20 个不同的基准有多关心？” (00:14:55)：有些公司，他们看到这些基准，他们会说，“好吧，出于公关目的，尽管我们认为这些学术基准并不那么重要，但也许我们只是需要对它们进行优化，因为我们的营销团队需要在其他公司谈论的某些标准评估上取得一定的进展，如果我们在这里没有表现出良好的表现，那对我们来说将是不利的即使忽略这些学术基准会让我们在实际任务中做得更好。” (00:15:21)：其他公司会坚持原则，并表示，“好吧，是的，不，我不关心营销。我只关心我的模型在一天结束时在这些现实世界任务上的表现，因此我将对此进行优化。” (00:15:31)：这几乎就像所有这些不同的事情之间都存在权衡，并且就像...... (00:15:36)：我经常想到的一件事是......这几乎就像是一种发布训练的艺术。这不纯粹是一种当你决定要创建什么样的模型以及它擅长什么时，就会有这种品味和复杂性的概念，比如，“好吧，我认为这些......”（00:15:57）：那么回到模型在视觉设计方面有多好的例子，我想，“好吧，也许你对视觉设计的看法与我不同。也许你更关心极简主义，而且你比我更关心，我不知道，3D动画。也许这个人更喜欢看起来有点破烂的东西。”在设计训练后组合时，你必须在设计训练后组合时做出决定，因此这也很重要。（00:16:21）：长话短说，我认为存在所有这些不同的因素，当然数据是其中的重要组成部分，但这也就像你试图优化模型的目标函数是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. The taste of the person leading this work will inform what data they ask for, what data they feed it. But it's wild it shows the value of great data. Anthropic got so much growth and win from essentially better data.
turns.zh: 那太有趣了。领导这项工作的人的品味将决定他们需要什么数据，他们提供什么数据。但这很疯狂，它显示了大数据的价值。 Anthropic 获得了如此大的增长并从本质上更好的数据中获胜。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I could see why companies like yours are growing so fast. There's just so much... And that's just one vertical. That's just coding, and then there's probably a similar area for writing. I love that it's... It's interesting that AI, it feels like this artificial computer binary thing, but it's like taste. Human judgment is still such a key factor in these things being successful.
turns.zh: 我明白为什么像你们这样的公司发展得如此之快。实在是太多了……而这只是一个垂直领域。这只是编码，然后可能还有类似的写作领域。我喜欢它……人工智能很有趣，感觉就像是人造计算机二进制的东西，但它就像味道。人类的判断仍然是这些事情成功的关键因素。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yep, exactly. Again, going back to the example I said earlier, certain companies, if you ask them what is good poem, they will simply robotically check off all of these instructions on our list. (00:17:20): But again, I don't think that makes for good poetry, so certain frontier labs, the ones with more taste in sophistication, they will realize that it doesn't reduce to this six set of checkboxes and they'll consider all of these kind of implicit, very subtle qualities instead, and I think that's what makes them better at this at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。再次回到我之前说的例子，某些公司，如果你问他们什么是好诗，他们会简单地自动勾选我们列表上的所有这些说明。 (00:17:20)：但是，我不认为这会带来好的诗歌，所以某些前沿实验室，那些在复杂性上更有品味的实验室，他们会意识到它不会减少到这六组复选框，而是会考虑所有这些隐含的、非常微妙的品质，我认为这就是让他们最终在这方面做得更好的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned benchmarks. This is something a lot of people worry about is there's all these models that are always... Basically, it feels like every model is better than humans at every STEM field at this point, but to a regular person, it doesn't feel like these models are getting that much smarter constantly. What's your just sense of how much you trust benchmarks and just how correlated those are with actual AI advancements?
turns.zh: 您提到了基准。这是很多人担心的事情，所有这些模型总是......基本上，在这一点上，感觉每个模型在每个 STEM 领域都比人类更好，但对于普通人来说，并不觉得这些模型不断变得那么聪明。您对基准的信任程度以及基准与实际人工智能进步的相关程度如何？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, so I don't trust the benchmarks at all. And I think that's for two reasons. So one is I think a lot of people don't realize, even researchers within the community, they don't realize that the benchmarks themselves are often honestly just wrong. They have wrong answers. They're full of all this kind of messiness and people trust... Long as for the popular ones, people have maybe realized this to some extent, but the vast majority just have all these flaws that people don't realize. So that's one part of it. (00:18:30): And the other part of it is these benchmarks at the end of the day, they often have well-defined objective answers that make them very easy for models to hill-climb on in a way that's very different from the messiness and ambiguity of the real world. (00:18:48): I think one thing that I often say is that it's kind of crazy that these models can win IMO gold medals, but they still have trouble parsing PDFs. And that's because, yeah, even though IMO gold medals seem hard to the average person, yeah, they are hard at the end of the day. But they have this notion of objectivity that, okay, yeah, parsing a PDF sometimes doesn't have. And so it's easier for the frontier labs to hill-climb on all of these than to solve all these mess ambiguous problems in the real world. So I think there's a lack of direct correlation there.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我根本不相信基准。我认为这有两个原因。因此，我认为很多人都没有意识到，即使是社区内的研究人员，他们也没有意识到基准本身往往是诚实的错误的。他们的答案是错误的。它们充满了这种混乱和人们的信任……只要是流行的，人们可能已经在某种程度上意识到了这一点，但绝大多数只是存在人们没有意识到的所有这些缺陷。这就是其中的一部分。 (00:18:30)：另一部分是归根结底的这些基准，它们通常有明确定义的客观答案，使模型很容易以一种与现实世界的混乱和模糊性截然不同的方式爬山。 (00:18:48)：我认为我经常说的一件事是，这些模型能够赢得 IMO 金牌，但它们在解析 PDF 时仍然遇到困难，这有点疯狂。那是因为，是的，尽管国际海事组织金牌对普通人来说似乎很难，是的，归根结底它们很难。但他们有客观性的概念，好吧，是的，解析 PDF 有时没有这种概念。因此，对于前沿实验室来说，解决所有这些问题比解决现实世界中所有这些混乱且模糊的问题更容易。所以我认为那里缺乏直接相关性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting the way you described it is hitting these benchmarks is kind of like a marketing piece. When you launch, say Gemini 3 just launched, and it's like, cool. Number one with all these benchmarks. Is that what happens? They just kind of train their models to get good at these very specific things?
turns.zh: 你所描述的达到这些基准的方式非常有趣，有点像营销作品。当你发布时，假设 Gemini 3 刚刚发布，感觉很酷。在所有这些基准中排名第一。是这样吗？他们只是训练他们的模型来擅长这些非常具体的事情？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, so there's, again, maybe two parts to this. So one is, sometimes, yeah, these benchmarks, they accidentally leak in certain ways or the frontier labs will tweak the way they evaluate their models on these benchmarks. They'll tweak your system prompt or they'll tweak the number of times they run their model, and so on and so on in a way that games these benchmarks. (00:19:54): The other part of it though is it's like by optimizing for the benchmark instead of optimizing for the real world, you will just naturally climb on the benchmark and, yeah, it's basically another form of gaming it.
turns.zh: 是的，所以，这可能又分为两个部分。所以，有时，是的，这些基准测试，他们会以某些方式意外泄漏，或者前沿实验室会调整他们在这些基准测试上评估模型的方式。他们会调整您的系统提示，或者调整运行模型的次数，等等，以符合这些基准的方式。 (00:19:54)：另一方面，就像通过针对基准进行优化而不是针对现实世界进行优化一样，你会自然地攀登基准，是的，这基本上是另一种形式的游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Knowing that with that in mind, how do you get a sense of if we're heading towards AGI, how do you measure progress?
turns.zh: 考虑到这一点，你如何了解我们是否正在走向通用人工智能，你如何衡量进展？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yes, so the way we really care about measuring model progress is by running all these human evaluations. (00:20:21): So for example, what we do is, yeah, we will take Gore human annotators, and we'll ask them, "Okay, go have a conversational model." And maybe you're having this conversation with the model across all of these different topics. So you are a Nobel Prize winning physicist. So you go have a conversation about pushing different tier of your own research. You are a teacher and you're trying to create lesson plans for your students, so go talk to the model about these things. Or you're a coder and you're working at one of these big tech companies, and you have these problems every day, so go talk to the model and see how much it helps you. (00:20:57): And because or searchers or annotators, they are experts at the top of their fields, and they are not just giving your responses, they're actually working through the responses deeply themselves, they are... Yeah, they're going to evaluate the code that it write. They're going to double check the physics equations that it writes. They're going to evaluate the models in a very deep way, so they're going to pay attention to accuracy and instruction following, all these things that casual users don't when you suddenly get a popup on your ChatGPT response asking you to compare these two different responses. People like that, they're not evaluating models deeply, they're just vibing and picking whatever response looks flashiest or [inaudible 00:21:38] are looking closely at responses and evaluating them for all of these different dimensions, and so I think that's a much better approach than these benchmarks or these random outline AV tests.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我们真正关心衡量模型进度的方式是运行所有这些人工评估。 (00:20:21)：例如，我们所做的是，是的，我们将采用戈尔人类注释者，我们会问他们，“好吧，去建立一个对话模型。”也许您正在与模特就所有这些不同的主题进行对话。所以你是一位获得诺贝尔奖的物理学家。所以你们去讨论一下推动自己不同层次的研究。您是一名老师，正在尝试为学生制定课程计划，因此请与模特讨论这些事情。或者你是一名程序员，在这些大型科技公司之一工作，你每天都会遇到这些问题，所以去与模型交谈，看看它对你有多大帮助。 (00:20:57)：因为搜索者或注释者，他们是各自领域的顶尖专家，他们不仅仅是给出你的回复，他们实际上自己也在深入研究这些回复，他们......是的，他们将评估它编写的代码。他们将仔细检查它所写的物理方程。他们将以非常深入的方式评估模型，因此他们将关注准确性和指令遵循，当你突然在 ChatGPT 响应中弹出一个弹出窗口，要求你比较这两个不同的响应时，普通用户不会关注所有这些事情。像这样的人，他们不会深入评估模型，他们只是振动并选择任何看起来最华丽的响应，或者 [听不清 00:21:38] 仔细观察响应并评估它们的所有这些不同维度，所以我认为这是比这些基准或这些随机轮廓 AV 测试更好的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Again, I love just how central humans continue to be in all this work that we're not totally done yet. Is there going to be a point where we don't need these people anymore, that AI is so smart that, "Okay, we're good. We got everything out of your heads"?
turns.zh: 再说一次，我喜欢人类在我们尚未完全完成的所有工作中继续发挥的核心作用。是否会有一天，我们不再需要这些人，人工智能是如此聪明，以至于“好吧，我们很好。我们把你脑子里的一切都弄清楚了”？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, I think that will not happen until we've reached AGI. It's almost like by definition, if we haven't reached AGI yet, then there's more for the models to learn from, and so, yeah, I don't think that's going to happen anytime soon.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为在我们达到通用人工智能之前这不会发生。这几乎就像根据定义，如果我们还没有达到 AGI，那么模型就有更多东西可以学习，所以，是的，我认为这不会很快发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So more reason to stress about AGI. "We don't need these folks anymore." (00:22:18): I can't not ask just... People that work closely with this stuff, I'm always just curious. What's your AGI timelines? How far do you think we are from this? Do you think we're in like a couple years or is it like decades?
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。因此更有理由强调 AGI。 “我们不再需要这些人了。” (00:22:18)：我不能不问……对于那些与这些东西密切合作的人，我总是很好奇。你们的 AGI 时间表是怎样的？您认为我们离这个目标还有多远？你认为我们的时间是几年还是几十年？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: So I'm certainly on the longer time horizon front. I think people don't realize that there's a big difference between moving from 80% performance to 90% performance to 99% performance to 99.9% performance, and so on, and so on. And so in my head, I probably bet that within the next one or two years, yeah, the models are going to automate 80% of the average LL6 software engineer's job. It's going to take another few years to move to 90%, and another fewer to 99%, and so on, and so on. So I think we're closer to a decade or decades away than [inaudible 00:23:03].
turns.zh: 所以我当然站在更长远的角度。我认为人们没有意识到从 80% 性能到 90% 性能到 99% 性能到 99.9% 性能等等之间存在很大差异。所以在我看来，我可能打赌在接下来的一两年内，是的，这些模型将使 LL6 软件工程师平均 80% 的工作实现自动化。还需要几年时间才能达到 90%，再过几年才能达到 99%，以此类推。所以我认为我们比 [听不清 00:23:03] 更接近十年或几十年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this hot take that a lot of these labs are kind of pushing AGI in the wrong direction and this is based on your work at Twitter, and Google, and Facebook. Can you just talk about that?
turns.zh: 你有一个强烈的观点，即许多实验室都在将 AGI 推向错误的方向，这是基于你在 Twitter、谷歌和 Facebook 的工作。你能简单谈谈吗？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I'm worried that instead of building AI that will actually advance us as a species, curing cancer, solving poverty, understand the universe, all these big grand questions, we are optimizing for AI slop instead. We're basically teaching our models to chase dopamine instead of truth. And I think this relates to what we're talking about regarding these benchmarks. So let me give you a couple examples. (00:23:35): So right now, the industry is played by these terrible databoards like LLM Arena. It's this popular online leaderboard where random people from around the world vote on which AI response is better. But the thing is, like I was saying earlier, they're not carefully reading or fact-checking. They're skimming these responses for two seconds and picking whatever looks flashiest. (00:23:53): So a model can hallucinate everything. It can completely hallucinate. But it will look impressive because it has crazy emojis, and boating, and markdown headers, and all these superficial things that don't matter at all, but it catch your attention. And these LLM-reading users love it. It's literally optimizing your models for the types of people who buy tabloids at the grocery store. We've seen this [inaudible 00:24:15] data ourselves. The easiest way to climb LLM Arena, it's adding crazy boating. It's doubling the number of emojis. It's tripling the length of your model responses, even if your model starts hallucinating and getting the answer completely wrong. (00:24:26): And the problem is, again, because all of these frontier labs, they kind of have to pay attention to PR because their sales team, when they're trying to sell to all these enterprise customers, those enterprise customers will say, "Oh, well, but your model's only number five on LLM Arena, so why should I buy it?" They have to, in some sense, pay attention to these leaderboards, and so what their researchers [inaudible 00:24:47] tell us is like they'll say, "The only way I'm going to get promoted at the end of the year is if I climb this leaderboard, even though I know that climbing it is probably going to make my model worse and accuracy [inaudible 00:24:57] following." So I think there's all these negative incentives that are pushing work in the wrong direction. (00:25:03): I'm also worried about this trend towards optimizing AI for engagement. I used to work on social media. And every time we optimize for engagement, terrible things happened. You'd get clickbait and pictures of bikinis and bigfoot and horrifying skin diseases just filling your feeds. And I think I worry that the same thing's happening with AI. If you think about all the sycophancy issues with ChatGPT, "Oh, you're absolutely right. What an amazing question," the easiest way to hook users is to tell them how amazing they are. And so these models, they constantly tell you you're a genius. They'll feed into your delusions and conspiracy theories. They'll pull you down these rabbit holes because Silicon Valley loves maximizing time spent and just increasing the number of conversations you're having with it. And so yeah, companies are spending all the time hacking these leaderboards and benchmarks, and the scores are going up, but I think it actually masks up the models with the best scores, they are often the worst or just have all these fundamental failures. So I think I'm really worried that all of these negative ascendants are pushing AGI into the wrong direction.
turns.zh: 我担心的是，我们并没有构建真正能够推动人类进步、治愈癌症、解决贫困、理解宇宙以及所有这些重大问题的人工智能，而是针对人工智能的问题进行了优化。我们基本上是在教我们的模型追逐多巴胺而不是真相。我认为这与我们所讨论的这些基准相关。让我举几个例子。 (00:23:35)：所以现在，这个行业被 LLM Arena 等可怕的数据板所左右。这是一个流行的在线排行榜，来自世界各地的随机人们可以投票选出哪个人工智能响应更好。但问题是，正如我之前所说，他们没有仔细阅读或核实事实。他们会花两秒钟浏览这些回复，然后选择看起来最华丽的内容。 (00:23:53)：所以模型可以产生一切幻觉。它可以完全产生幻觉。但它看起来会令人印象深刻，因为它有疯狂的表情符号、划船和降价标题，以及所有这些根本不重要的肤浅的东西，但它引起了你的注意。这些 LLM 阅读用户喜欢它。它实际上是针对在杂货店购买小报的人群类型优化您的模型。我们自己已经看到了这个 [听不清 00:24:15] 数据。攀登LLM Arena最简单的方法就是添加疯狂划船。表情符号的数量增加了一倍。即使您的模型开始出现幻觉并得到完全错误的答案，它也会使模型响应的长度增加两倍。 (00:24:26)：问题又是，因为所有这些前沿实验室，他们都必须关注公关，因为他们的销售团队，当他们试图向所有这些企业客户销售产品时，这些企业客户会说，“哦，好吧，但你的模型在 LLM Arena 上只排名第五，所以我为什么要买它？”从某种意义上说，他们必须关注这些排行榜，因此他们的研究人员 [听不清 00:24:47] 告诉我们的就像他们会说的那样，“我在年底升职的唯一方法就是攀登这个排行榜，尽管我知道攀登它可能会让我的模型变得更糟，并且准确性 [听不清 00:24:57] 接下来。”所以我认为所有这些负面激励措施正在将工作推向错误的方向。 (00:25:03)：我也担心这种优化人工智能以提高参与度的趋势。我曾经在社交媒体上工作。每次我们优化参与度时，可怕的事情都会发生。你会收到标题诱饵、比基尼、大脚怪和可怕的皮肤病的图片，这些都充斥着你的提要。我想我担心人工智能也会发生同样的事情。如果你考虑一下 ChatGPT 的所有阿谀奉承问题，“哦，你完全正确。这是一个多么令人惊奇的问题”，吸引用户的最简单方法就是告诉他们他们有多么了不起。所以这些模特，他们不断地告诉你，你是个天才。它们会助长你的妄想和阴谋论。他们会把你拉进这些兔子洞，因为硅谷喜欢最大化花费的时间，并增加你与之进行的对话的数量。所以，是的，公司一直在花时间破解这些排行榜和基准，分数正在上升，但我认为这实际上掩盖了分数最高的模型，它们往往是最差的，或者只是有所有这些根本性的失败。所以我认为我真的很担心所有这些负面因素正在将 AGI 推向错误的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is AGI is being slowed down by these, basically the wrong objective function, these labs paying attention to the wrong basically benchmarks and evals.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是 AGI 正在被这些基本上错误的目标函数拖慢，这些实验室基本上关注错误的基准和评估。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you probably can't play favorites since you work with all the labs. Is there anyone doing better at this and maybe kind of realizing this is the wrong direction?
turns.zh: 我知道您可能无法偏爱，因为您与所有实验室一起工作。有没有人在这方面做得更好，并且可能意识到这是错误的方向？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I would say I've always been very impressed by Anthropic. I think Anthropic takes a very principled view about what they do and don't care about and how they want their models to behave in a way that feels a lot more principle to me.
turns.zh: 我想说，Anthropic 一直给我留下了深刻的印象。我认为 Anthropic 对他们做什么、不关心什么以及他们希望模型如何以一种对我来说更有原则性的方式表现持非常原则性的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. (00:26:39): Are there any other big mistakes you think labs are making just that are kind of slowing things down or heading in the wrong direction? Where we've heard just chasing benchmarks, this engagement focus, is there anything else you're seeing of just like, "Okay, we got to work on this because it'll speed everything up"?
turns.zh: 有趣的。 (00:26:39)：您认为实验室是否还犯有其他重大错误，这些错误会减慢进度或走向错误的方向？我们听说过只是追逐基准、这种参与焦点，但您是否还看到过其他类似的内容，比如“好吧，我们必须努力解决这个问题，因为它会加快一切速度”？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I think there is a question of what products they're building and whether those products themselves are something that kind of help or hurt humanity. I think a lot about Sora and...
turns.zh: 我认为存在的问题是他们正在制造什么产品以及这些产品本身是否有助于或伤害人类。我对索拉想了很多，还有……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was thinking that's what you're imagining.
turns.zh: 我以为这就是你所想象的。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, what it entails, and so it's kind of interesting. It's like which companies would build Sora and which wouldn't? (00:27:17): And I think that answer to that... Well, I don't know if answer is myself. I have an idea in my head, but I think the answer to that question maybe reveals certain things about what kinds of AI models those companies want to build and what direction and what future they want to achieve, yeah, so I think about that a lot.
turns.zh: 是的，它意味着什么，所以这很有趣。就像哪些公司会建造 Sora，哪些公司不会？ (00:27:17)：我认为这个问题的答案...好吧，我不知道答案是否是我自己。我脑子里有一个想法，但我认为这个问题的答案可能揭示了这些公司想要构建什么样的人工智能模型以及他们想要实现什么方向和未来的某些信息，是的，所以我想了很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The steel man argument there is, it's like fun, people want it, it'll help them generate revenue to grow this thing and build better models, it'll train data in an interesting way, it's also just really fun.
turns.zh: 钢铁侠的论点是，这很有趣，人们想要它，它将帮助他们产生收入来发展这个东西并建立更好的模型，它将以一种有趣的方式训练数据，这也非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah. I think it's almost like, do you care about how you get there? And in the same way, so I made this tabloid analogy earlier, but would you sell tabloids in order to fund, I don't know, some other newspaper? (00:28:09): Sure, like in some sense, if you don't care about the path, then you'll just do whatever it takes, but it's possible that it has negative consequences in of itself that will harm the long-term direction of what you're trying to achieve, and maybe it'll distract you from all the more important things, so yeah, I think that the path you take matters a lot as well.
turns.zh: 是的。我想这几乎就像是，你关心如何到达那里吗？同样，我之前做了这个小报的类比，但是你会出售小报来资助其他报纸吗？我不知道？ (00:28:09)：当然，从某种意义上说，如果你不关心这条路，那么你就会不惜一切代价，但它本身可能会产生负面后果，会损害你想要实现的目标的长期方向，也许它会分散你对所有更重要事情的注意力，所以是的，我认为你所走的路也很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, you talked a bunch about this of just Silicon Valley and kind of the downsides of raising a lot of money being in the echo chamber. What do you call it, the Silicon Valley machine? You talk about how it's hard to build important companies in this way and that you might actually be much more successful if you're not going down the VC path. Can you just talk about what you've seen in that experience and your advice essentially to founders, because they're always hearing? Raise money from fancy VCs, move to Silicon Valley, what's kind of the countertake?
turns.zh: 沿着这些思路，你谈到了很多关于硅谷的事情，以及在回声室中筹集大量资金的缺点。你怎么称呼它，硅谷机器？你谈到以这种方式建立重要的公司是多么困难，如果你不走风险投资的道路，你实际上可能会更成功。您能否谈谈您在那次经历中看到的情况以及您对创始人的建议，因为他们总是在倾听？从高级风险投资公司筹集资金，搬到硅谷，什么样的反击？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yes. So I've always really hated a lot of the Silicon Valley mantras. The standard playbook is to get product market fit by pivoting every two weeks. And to chase growth and chase engagement with all of these dark patterns and to blitz scale by hiring as fast as possible. And I've always disagreed. (00:29:20): So yeah, I would say don't pivot. Don't put scale. Don't hire that Stanford grad who simply wants to add a hot company to your resume, just build the one thing only you could build, a thing that wouldn't exist without the insight and expertise that only you have. (00:29:32): And you see these buy to [inaudible 00:29:34] companies everywhere now. Some founder who was doing crypto in 2020, and then pivoted to NFTs in 2022, and now they're an AI company. There's no consistency, there's no mission, they're just chasing valuations. And I've always hated this because Silicon Valley loves to score on Wall Street for focusing on money. But honestly, most of the Silicon Valley's chasing the same thing. And so we stayed focused on our mission from day one, pushing that frontier of high quality complex data, and I've always loved that because I think startups... (00:30:03): I have this very romantic notion of startups. Startups are supposed to be a way of taking big risks to build something that you really believe in. But if you're constantly pivoting, you're not taking any risks. You're just trying to make a quick buck. And if you fail because the market isn't ready yet, I actually think that's way better. At least you took a swing at something deep, and novel, and hard instead of pivoting into another LLM wrapper company. So yeah, I think the only way you build something that matters that's going to change the world is if you find a big idea you believe in and you say no to everything else. (00:30:30): So you don't keep on pivoting when it gets hard, you don't hire a team of 10 product managers because that's what every other cookie cutter startup does, you just keep building that one company that wouldn't exist without you. And I think there are a lot of people in Silicon Valley now who are sick of all the grift, who want to work on big things that matter with people who actually care, and I'm hoping that that would be the future of how we go with technology.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我一直非常讨厌硅谷的很多口头禅。标准的策略是通过每两周调整一次来使产品适应市场。为了追求增长并追求所有这些黑暗模式的参与，并通过尽快招聘来实现闪电式扩张。而我一直不同意。 (00:29:20)：是的，我想说不要转向。不要放刻度。不要雇用那个只想在你的简历中添加一家热门公司的斯坦福大学毕业生，只需构建只有你才能构建的东西，如果没有只有你拥有的洞察力和专业知识，它就不会存在。 (00:29:32)：现在你会看到这些人向[听不清 00:29:34] 公司购买产品。一些创始人在 2020 年做加密货币，然后在 2022 年转向 NFT，现在他们是一家人工智能公司。没有一致性，没有使命，他们只是追逐估值。我一直讨厌这一点，因为硅谷喜欢因为专注于金钱而在华尔街上得分。但老实说，大多数硅谷人都在追求同样的事情。因此，我们从第一天起就专注于我们的使命，推动高质量复杂数据的前沿，我一直很喜欢这一点，因为我认为初创公司...... (00:30:03)：我对初创公司有一种非常浪漫的想法。初创公司应该是一种冒巨大风险来打造你真正相信的东西的方式。但如果你不断地调整方向，你就不会冒任何风险。你只是想赚快钱。如果你因为市场还没有准备好而失败，我实际上认为那更好。至少你尝试了一些有深度、新颖、困难的东西，而不是转向另一家法学硕士包装公司。所以，是的，我认为你建立一些能够改变世界的重要东西的唯一方法就是找到一个你相信的伟大想法并对其他一切说不。 (00:30:30)：所以当事情变得困难时，你不会继续转型，你不会雇佣一个由 10 名产品经理组成的团队，因为这就是其他千篇一律的初创公司所做的，你只是继续建立一家没有你就不会存在的公司。我认为现在硅谷有很多人厌倦了所有的欺骗，他们想要与真正关心的人一起做重要的事情，我希望这将是我们如何使用技术的未来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm actually working on a post right now with Terrence Rohan, this VC that I really like to work with, and we interviewed five people who picked really successful generational companies early and joined them as really early employees. They joined OpenAI before anyone thought it was awesome, Stripe before anyone knew was awesome, and so we're looking for patterns of how people find these generational companies before anyone else, and it aligns exactly what you described, which is ambition. They have a wild ambition with what they want to achieve. They're not, as you said, just kind of looking around for product market fit no matter what ends up being, and so I love that what you described very much aligns with what we're seeing there.
turns.zh: 实际上，我现在正在与泰伦斯·罗汉（Terrence Rohan）一起工作，他是我非常喜欢与之合作的风险投资家，我们采访了五个人，他们很早就选择了真正成功的代际公司，并作为真正的早期员工加入了他们。他们在人们认为 OpenAI 很棒之前就加入了，在人们知道 Stripe 很棒之前就加入了，所以我们正在寻找人们如何先于其他人找到这些一代公司的模式，它与你所描述的完全一致，这就是雄心。他们对自己想要实现的目标有着野心。正如您所说，他们并不是只是四处寻找适合市场的产品，无论最终结果如何，所以我喜欢您所描述的内容与我们在那里看到的非常一致。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen

(00:42:35): And then there's this other notion of evals where you're trying to measure the model's progress like, okay, yeah, I have five different candidate checkpoints and I want to pick the one that's best in order to release it to the public. So going to run all these evals on these five different checkpoints in order to decide which one is best.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我认为评估通常涵盖两个术语。一是您使用评估进行训练，因为您正在评估模型是否做得很好，当它确实做得很好时，您就会奖励它。 (00:42:35)：然后还有另一种评估概念，你试图衡量模型的进度，就像，好吧，是的，我有五个不同的候选检查点，我想选择最好的一个，以便将其发布给公众。因此，将对这五个不同的检查点运行所有这些评估，以确定哪一个最好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 惊人的。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, and now we have RL environments, so this is kind of like a hot new thing.
turns.zh: 是的，现在我们有了强化学习环境，所以这有点像一个热门的新事物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So what I love about this business journey is just there's always something new. There's always this like, okay. We're getting so good at just all this beautiful data for companies and now they need something completely different. Now we're setting up all these virtual machines for them and all these different use cases.
turns.zh: 惊人的。所以我喜欢这次商业之旅的原因就是总是有新的东西。总有这样的事，好吧。我们已经非常擅长为公司提供所有这些美丽的数据，而现在他们需要完全不同的东西。现在我们正在为它们和所有这些不同的用例设置所有这些虚拟机。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like that's a big part of this industry you're in, it's just adapting to what labs are asking for.
turns.zh: 感觉这是您所在行业的重要组成部分，它只是适应实验室的要求。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah. So I really do think that we are going to need to build a suite of products that reflect a million different ways that humans learn. (00:43:25): Like for example, think about becoming a great writer. You don't become great by memorizing a bunch of grammar rules. You become great by reading great books, and you practice writing, and you get feedback from your teachers and from the people who buy your books in a bookstore and leave reviews. And you notice what works and what doesn't. And you develop taste by being exposed to all of these masterpieces and also just terrible writing. So you learn through this endless cycle of practicing reflection, and each type of learning that you have, again, these are all very different methods of learning to become a great writer, so just in the same way that... it's a thousand different ways that the great writer becomes great, I think there's going to be a thousand different ways that AI [inaudible 00:44:05] need to learn.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我确实认为我们需要构建一套产品来反映人类一百万种不同的学习方式。 (00:43:25)：例如，考虑成为一名伟大的作家。记住一堆语法规则并不能让你变得伟大。你通过阅读好书而变得伟大，你练习写作，你从你的老师和在书店购买你的书并留下评论的人那里得到反馈。你会注意到什么有效，什么无效。通过接触所有这些杰作和糟糕的写作，你可以培养品味。所以你通过这个无休止的练习反思的循环来学习，你所拥有的每种类型的学习，同样，这些都是学习成为一名伟大作家的非常不同的方法，所以就像......伟大作家变得伟大有一千种不同的方式一样，我认为人工智能[听不清00:44:05]需要学习一千种不同的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting this just ends up being just like humans in so many ways. It makes sense because in a sense, neural networks, deep learning is modeled after how humans have learned and how our brains operate, but it's interesting just to make them smarter. It's how do we come closer to how humans learn more and more?
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，它最终在很多方面都像人类一样。这是有道理的，因为从某种意义上说，神经网络、深度学习是按照人类的学习方式和大脑的运作方式建模的，但仅仅让它们变得更聪明就很有趣。我们如何才能越来越接近人类学习的方式？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, it's almost like maybe the end goal is just throwing you into the environment and just seeing how you evolve. But within that evolution, there's all these different sub-learning mechanisms.
turns.zh: 是的，这几乎就像最终目标只是把你扔到环境中，看看你如何进化。但在这种演变中，存在着所有这些不同的子学习机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, which is kind of what we're doing now, so that's really interesting. This might be the last step until we hit AGI. Along these lines, something that's really unique to Surge that I learned is you guys have your own research team, which I think is pretty rare, talk about just why that's something you guys have invested in and what has come out of that investment.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是我们现在正在做的事情，所以这真的很有趣。这可能是我们实现 AGI 之前的最后一步。沿着这些思路，我了解到 Surge 真正独特的一点是，你们拥有自己的研究团队，我认为这是相当罕见的，请谈谈你们投资的原因以及投资的结果。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, so I think that stems from my own background. My own background is as a researcher. And so I've always cared fundamentally about pushing the industry and pushing the research community and not just about revenue. And so I think what our research team does is a couple different things. (00:45:13): So we almost have two types of researchers at our company. One is our forward-deployed researchers who are often working hand in hand with our customers to help them understand their models. So we will work very closely with the customers to help them understand, "Okay, this is where your model is today. This is where you're lagging behind all the competitors, these are some ways that you could be improving in the future, given your goals, and we're going to design these data sets, these evaluation methods, these training techniques to make your models better." So this very collaborative notion of working with our customers being researched by themselves, just a little bit more focused on the data side, and working hand on hand with them to do whatever it takes to make them the best. (00:45:57): And then we also have our internal researchers. So our internal researchers are focused on slightly different things. So they are focused on building better benchmarks and better leaderboards. (00:46:07): So I've talked a lot about how I worry that the leaderboards and benchmarks out there today are steering models in the wrong direction, so yeah, so the question is, how do we fix that? And so that's what our research team is focused focused really heavily on right now. So they're working a lot on that. (00:46:23): And they're also working on these other things like, "Okay, we need to train our own models to see what types of data performs the best, what types of people perform the best." And so they're also working on all these training techniques and evaluation of our own data sets to improve our data operations and the internal data products that we have that determine what makes something good quality.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我认为这源于我自己的背景。我自己的背景是一名研究员。因此，我一直从根本上关心推动行业和研究界的发展，而不仅仅是收入。所以我认为我们的研究团队所做的是几件不同的事情。 (00:45:13)：所以我们公司几乎有两种类型的研究人员。其中之一是我们前沿部署的研究人员，他们经常与我们的客户携手合作，帮助他们理解他们的模型。因此，我们将与客户密切合作，帮助他们理解，“好吧，这就是你的模型现在的情况。这就是你落后于所有竞争对手的地方，根据你的目标，这些是你未来可以改进的一些方法，我们将设计这些数据集、这些评估方法、这些训练技术来使你的模型变得更好。”因此，这种非常协作的理念是与我们的客户一起进行研究，稍微关注数据方面，并与他们携手合作，尽一切努力使他们做到最好。 (00:45:57)：我们还有内部研究人员。因此，我们的内部研究人员关注的事情略有不同。因此，他们专注于建立更好的基准和更好的排行榜。 (00:46:07)：所以我已经谈了很多关于我如何担心当今的排行榜和基准将模型引向错误的方向，所以是的，所以问题是，我们如何解决这个问题？这就是我们的研究团队目前重点关注的问题。所以他们在这方面做了很多工作。 (00:46:23)：他们还在研究其他事情，比如“好吧，我们需要训练我们自己的模型，看看什么类型的数据表现最好，什么类型的人表现最好。”因此，他们也在研究所有这些培训技术和对我们自己的数据集的评估，以改进我们的数据操作和我们拥有的内部数据产品，这些产品决定了哪些东西是优质的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a cool thing because I don't think basically the labs have researchers helping them advance AI. I imagine it's pretty rare for a company like yours to have researchers actually doing primary research on AI.
turns.zh: 这是一件很酷的事情，因为我认为实验室基本上没有研究人员帮助他们推进人工智能。我想像你们这样的公司很少有研究人员真正对人工智能进行初步研究。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's just because it's something I've fundamentally always cared about. I often think about us more like a research lab than a startup because that is my goal. It's kind of funny, but I've always said I would rather be Terrence Tau than Warren Buffett, so that notion of creating research that pushes the frontier forward and not just getting some valuation, that's always been what drives me.
turns.zh: 是的，我想这只是因为这是我从根本上一直关心的事情。我经常认为我们更像是一个研究实验室，而不是一家初创公司，因为这是我的目标。这有点有趣，但我总是说我宁愿成为泰伦斯·陶而不是沃伦·巴菲特，因此，创造推动前沿发展的研究而不仅仅是获得一些估值的想法一直是我的动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's worked out. That's the beautiful thing about this. You mentioned that you were hiring researchers, is there anything there you want to share folks you're looking for?
turns.zh: 事情已经解决了。这就是这件事的美妙之处。您提到您正在招聘研究人员，您有什么想与您分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: So we look for people who are just fundamentally interested in dataset all day. So types of people who could literally spend 10 hours digging through a dataset, and playing around with models, and thinking, "Okay, yeah, this is where I think the model's failing," this is the kind of a behavior you want the model to have instead, and just this aspect of being very hands-on and thinking about the qualitative aspects of models and not just the quantitative parts. So again, it's like this aspect of being hands-on with data and not just caring about these kind of abstract algorithms.
turns.zh: 因此，我们寻找整天对数据集有根本兴趣的人。因此，那些可以花 10 个小时挖掘数据集、摆弄模型并思考“好吧，是的，这就是我认为模型失败的地方”的人，这就是你希望模型具有的行为，而这就是非常亲力亲为并思考模型的定性方面而不仅仅是定量部分。再说一遍，这就像亲自动手处理数据，而不仅仅是关心这些抽象算法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. (00:48:07): I want to ask a couple broad AI kind of market questions. What else do you think is coming in the next couple of years that people are maybe not thinking enough about or not expecting in terms of where AI is heading? What's going to matter?
turns.zh: 惊人的。 (00:48:07)：我想问一些广泛的人工智能市场问题。您认为未来几年还会有哪些事情是人们对人工智能的发展方向没有充分思考或没有预期的？有什么关系呢？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I think one of the things that's going to happen in the next few years is that the models are actually going to become increasingly differentiated because of the personalities and behaviors that the different labs have and the kind of objective functions that they are optimizing their models for. I think it's one thing I didn't appreciate a year or so ago. (00:48:45): A year or so ago, I thought that all of the AI models would essentially become very commoditized. They would all behave like each other, and sure, one of them might be slightly more intelligent in one way today, but sure, the other ones would catch up in the next few months. But I think over the past year, I've realized that the values that the companies have will shape the model. (00:49:09): So let me give you an example. So I was asking Claude to help me draft an email the other day, and it went through 30 different versions. And after 30 minutes, yeah, I think it really crafted me the perfect email, and I sent it. But then I realized that I spent 30 minutes doing something that didn't matter at all. Sure, now I got the perfect email, but I spent 30 minutes doing something I wouldn't have worried at all before, and this email probably didn't even move the needle on anything anyways. (00:49:35): So I think there's a deep question here, which is, if you could choose the perfect model behavior, which model would you want? Do you want a model that says, "You're absolutely right. There are definitely 20 more ways to improve this email," and it continues for 50 more iterations. And it sucks up all your time and engagement. Or do you want a model that's optimizing for your time and productivity and just says, "No, you need to stop. Your email's great. Just send it and move on with your day"? (00:49:59): And again, just because... In the same way that there's like a kind of a fork in a road between how you could choose how your model behaves for this question, it's like for every other question that models have, the kind of behavior that you want will fundamentally affect it. (00:50:17): It's almost like in the same way that when Google builds a search engine, it's very different from how Facebook would build a search engine, which is very different from how Apple would build a search engine. They all have their own principles and values and things that they're trying to achieve in the world that shape all the products that they're going to build. And in the same way, I think all the [inaudible 00:50:40] will start behaving very differently too.
turns.zh: 我认为未来几年将发生的事情之一是，由于不同实验室的个性和行为以及他们优化模型的目标函数类型，模型实际上将变得越来越差异化。我认为这是大约一年前我不欣赏的一件事。 (00:48:45)：大约一年前，我认为所有人工智能模型基本上都会变得非常商品化。他们都会表现得像彼此，当然，其中一个今天可能在某一方面稍微聪明一些，但可以肯定的是，其他人会在接下来的几个月内赶上。但我认为在过去的一年里，我意识到公司的价值观将塑造这种模式。 (00:49:09)：让我举个例子。所以那天我请 Claude 帮我起草一封电子邮件，它经历了 30 个不同的版本。 30 分钟后，是的，我认为它确实为我制作了一封完美的电子邮件，然后我发送了它。但后来我意识到我花了30分钟做了一些根本不重要的事情。当然，现在我收到了一封完美的电子邮件，但我花了 30 分钟做了一些我以前根本不会担心的事情，而且这封电子邮件可能根本没有任何进展。 (00:49:35)：所以我认为这里有一个深刻的问题，那就是，如果你可以选择完美的模型行为，你会想要哪个模型？你想要一个模型说：“你完全正确。肯定还有 20 种方法可以改进这封电子邮件”，并且它会继续进行 50 次迭代。它会占用你所有的时间和参与度。或者您是否想要一个能够优化您的时间和生产力的模型，并且只是说：“不，您需要停下来。您的电子邮件很棒。只需发送它并继续您的一天”？ (00:49:59)：再说一遍，只是因为......就像在如何选择模型对这个问题的行为之间存在一种岔路一样，就像模型所面临的所有其他问题一样，你想要的行为类型将从根本上影响它。 (00:50:17)：这几乎就像谷歌构建搜索引擎的方式一样，它与 Facebook 构建搜索引擎的方式非常不同，而 Facebook 构建搜索引擎的方式也与苹果构建搜索引擎的方式非常不同。他们都有自己的原则和价值观，以及他们试图在世界上实现的目标，这些目标塑造了他们将要制造的所有产品。同样，我认为所有 [听不清 00:50:40] 的行为也会开始变得非常不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is incredibly interesting. You already see that with Grok. It's got a very different personality and a very different approach to answering questions. And so what I'm hearing is you're going to see more of this differentiation.
turns.zh: 这非常有趣。您已经在 Grok 中看到了这一点。它有非常不同的个性和非常不同的回答问题的方法。所以我听到的是，你会看到更多这种差异。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of another question along these lines, what do you think is most under-hyped in AI that you think maybe people aren't talking enough about that is really cool? And what do you think is over-hyped?
turns.zh: 与此类似的另一个问题是，你认为人工智能中最被低估的是什么，你认为人们可能没有足够地谈论这真的很酷？您认为什么被过度炒作了？

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: So I think one of the things that's under-hyped is the built-in products that all of the chatbots are going to start having. I've always been a huge fan of Claude's artifacts. And I think it just works really well. And actually the other day, I don't know if it's a new feature or not, but it asked me to help me create an email, and then it just created... So it didn't quite work because it didn't allow me to send the email. But what it created instead was like a little, I don't know what we call it, like a little box where I could click on it and it would just text someone that did this message. And I think that concept of taking artifacts to the next level where you just have these mini apps, mini UIs within the chatbots themselves, I feel like people aren't talking enough about that. So I think that that's one under-hyped area. (00:51:54): And in terms of over-hyped areas, I definitely think that vibe coding is over-hyped. I think people don't realize how much it's going to make your systems unmaintainable in the long-term and they simply dump this code into their code bases if this seems to work out right now, so I kind of worry about the future of coding. It's just going to keep on happening.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，其中一件被低估的事情是所有聊天机器人都将开始拥有的内置产品。我一直是克劳德手工艺品的忠实粉丝。我认为它效果非常好。实际上，有一天，我不知道这是否是一个新功能，但它要求我帮助我创建一封电子邮件，然后它就创建了......所以它不太有效，因为它不允许我发送电子邮件。但它创建的东西就像一个小盒子，我不知道我们叫它什么，就像一个小盒子，我可以点击它，它只会向发送此消息的人发送短信。我认为将工件提升到一个新水平的概念，在聊天机器人本身中拥有这些迷你应用程序、迷你用户界面，我觉得人们对此的讨论还不够。所以我认为这是一个未被充分宣传的领域。 (00:51:54)：就过度炒作的领域而言，我绝对认为氛围编码被过度炒作了。我认为人们没有意识到从长远来看这会让你的系统变得难以维护，如果现在看起来可行的话，他们只是将这些代码转储到他们的代码库中，所以我有点担心编码的未来。它只会继续发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are amazing answers. On that first point, there's something I actually asked. I have the chief product officer of Anthropic and OpenAI, Kevin Weil and Mike Krieger on the podcast, and I asked them just like, "As a product team, you have this gigabrain intelligence. How long do you even need product teams?" You think this AI will just create the product for you. "Here's what I want." It's like the next level of vibe coding. It's just like tell it, "Here's what I want," and it's just building the product and involving the product as you're using it. And it feels like that's what you're describing is where we might be heading.
turns.zh: 这些都是令人惊奇的答案。关于第一点，我实际上问过一些事情。我在播客上邀请了 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的首席产品官 Kevin Weil 和 Mike Krieger，我问他们，“作为一个产品团队，你们拥有这种超级智能。你们需要产品团队多久？”你认为这个人工智能只会为你创造产品。 “这就是我想要的。”这就像下一个级别的氛围编码。这就像告诉它，“这就是我想要的”，它只是构建产品并在您使用它时涉及该产品。感觉你所描述的就是我们可能前进的方向。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a very powerful notion where it helps people just achieve their ideas in a much cooler way.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为有一个非常强大的概念，它可以帮助人们以更酷的方式实现他们的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something we haven't gotten into that I think is really interesting is just the story of how you got to starting Surge. You have a really unique background. I always think about these... Brian Armstrong, the founder of Coinbase, once gave this talk that has really stuck with me where he kind of talked about how his very unique background allowed him to start Coinbase. He had a economics background, he had a cryptography experience, and then he was an engineer. And it's like the perfect Venn diagram for starting Coinbase, and I feel like you have a very similar story with Surge. Talk about that, your background there, and how that led to Surge.
turns.zh: 我们还没有讨论过一些我认为真正有趣的事情，那就是你如何开始 Surge 的故事。你有一个非常独特的背景。我一直在思考这些……Coinbase 的创始人布莱恩·阿姆斯特朗（Brian Armstrong）曾经做过一次让我印象深刻的演讲，他谈到了他独特的背景如何让他创办了 Coinbase。他有经济学背景，有密码学经验，然后他是一名工程师。这就像启动 Coinbase 的完美维恩图，我觉得 Surge 的故事非常相似。谈谈这个，你在那里的背景，以及这如何导致了 Surge。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: Going way back, I was always fascinated by math and language when I was a kid. I went to MIT because it's obviously one of the best places for math and CS, but also because it's the home of Noam Chomsky. My dream in school was actually to find some underlying theory connecting all these different fields. (00:53:47): And then I became a researcher at Google, and Facebook, and Twitter, and I just kept running into the same problem over and over again. It was impossible to get the data that we needed to train our models. So I was always this huge believer in the need for high quality data, and then GPT-3 came out in 2020. And I realized that, yeah, if we wanted to take things to the next level and build models that could code, and use tools, and tell jokes, and write poetry, and solve [inaudible 00:54:12], and cure cancer, then yeah, we were going to need a completely new solution. (00:54:16): The thing that always drove me crazy when I was at all these companies was we had a full power of the human mind in front of us, and all the data students out there were focused on really simple things like image labeling. So I wanted to build something focus on all these advanced, complex use cases instead that would really help us build our next generation models. So yeah, I think my background in kind of across math, and computer science, and linguistics really informed what I always wanted to do, and so I started Surge a month later with our one mission to basically build the use cases that I thought were going to be needed to push the frontier of AI.
turns.zh: 回想起来，当我还是个孩子的时候，我总是对数学和语言着迷。我去麻省理工学院是因为它显然是数学和计算机科学最好的地方之一，而且还因为它是诺姆·乔姆斯基的故乡。我在学校的梦想实际上是找到一些连接所有这些不同领域的基本理论。 (00:53:47)：然后我成为了谷歌、Facebook 和 Twitter 的研究员，我只是一遍又一遍地遇到同样的问题。我们无法获得训练模型所需的数据。所以我一直坚信需要高质量的数据，然后 GPT-3 在 2020 年问世。我意识到，是的，如果我们想要将事情提升到一个新的水平并构建可以编码、使用工具、讲笑话、写诗、解决问题 [听不清 00:54:12] 并治愈癌症的模型，那么是的，我们将需要一个全新的解决方案。 (00:54:16)：当我在所有这些公司时，总是让我发疯的是，我们面前拥有人类思维的全部力量，而且所有数据学生都专注于非常简单的事情，例如图像标签。因此，我想构建一些专注于所有这些高级、复杂用例的东西，而不是真正帮助我们构建下一代模型。所以，是的，我认为我在数学、计算机科学和语言学方面的背景确实告诉了我一直想做的事情，所以一个月后我开始了 Surge，我们的一个使命是基本上构建我认为推动人工智能前沿所需的用例。

I always thought I was going to become this math or CS professor and work on trying to understand the universe, and language, and the nature of communication. It's kind of funny, but I always had this fanciful dream where if aliens ever came to visit Earth and we need to figure out how to communicate with them, I wanted to be the one the government would call. And I'd use all this fancy math, and computer science, and linguistics to decipher it. (00:55:33): So even today, what I love doing most is every time a new model is released, we'll actually do a really deep dive into the model itself. I'll play around with it, I'll run evals, I'll compare where it's improved, where it's arrest, I'll create this really deep dive analysis that we send our customers. And it's actually kind of funny because a lot of times we'll say it's from a data science team, but often it's actually just from me. (00:55:54): And I think I could do this all day. I have a very hard time being in meetings all day. I'm terrible at sales, I'm terrible at doing the typical CEO things that people expect you to do, but I love writing these analyses. I love jamming with our research team about what we're seeing, sometimes I'll be up until 3:00 AM just talking on the phone with somebody on the research team and [inaudible 00:56:12] model. So I love that I still get to be really hands-on, working on the data and the science all day. And I think what drives me is that I want Surge to play this critical role in the future of AI, which I think is also the future of humanity. We have these really unique perspectives on data, and language, and quality, and how to measure all of this, and how to ensure it's all going on the right path. And I think we're uniquely unconstrained by all of these influences that can sometimes steer companies in a negative direction. turns.zh: 我想我本质上是一名科学家。我一直以为我会成为数学或计算机科学教授，努力理解宇宙、语言和交流的本质。这有点有趣，但我一直有一个幻想，如果外星人来到地球，我们需要弄清楚如何与他们沟通，我想成为政府打电话的那个人。我会使用所有这些奇特的数学、计算机科学和语言学来破译它。 (00:55:33)：所以即使在今天，我最喜欢做的就是每次发布新模型时，我们实际上都会深入研究模型本身。我将尝试它，我将运行评估，我将比较它的改进之处，它的停止之处，我将创建我们发送给客户的真正深入的深入分析。这实际上有点有趣，因为很多时候我们会说它来自数据科学团队，但实际上通常只是我自己。 (00:55:54)：我想我可以这样做一整天。我很难整天参加会议。我不擅长销售，也不擅长做人们期望你做的典型首席执行官的事情，但我喜欢写这些分析。我喜欢与我们的研究团队讨论我们所看到的内容，有时我会一直工作到凌晨 3:00，只是与研究团队的人员和 [听不清 00:56:12] 模型通电话。所以我喜欢我仍然能够真正亲自动手，整天研究数据和科学。我认为驱使我的是我希望 Surge 在人工智能的未来中发挥关键作用，我认为这也是人类的未来。我们对数据、语言和质量，以及如何衡量所有这些，以及如何确保一切都在正确的道路上进行，有着非常独特的视角。我认为我们独特地不受所有这些有时会引导公司走向负面方向的影响的限制。 (00:56:41)：就像我之前所说的，我们建立的 Surge 更像是一个研究实验室，而不是一家典型的初创公司。因此，我们关心的是好奇心、长期激励和智力严谨性，我们不太关心季度指标以及[听不清的 00:56:56] 看起来不错的内容。因此，我的目标是利用我们作为一家公司的所有这些独特之处，并利用它们来确保我们以一种从长远来看对我们人类真正有益的方式塑造人工智能。

turns.zh: 我在这次谈话中意识到，你们以及像你们这样的公司对人工智能的发展方向有多大的影响力。事实上，你帮助实验室了解他们的差距和需要改进的地方，不仅仅是每个人都像 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 以及所有这些公司的负责人一样看待他们，因为他们是人工智能的引领者，但我在这里听到的是，你对事情的发展也有很大的影响力。

turns.en: Yeah, I think there's this really powerful ecosystem where, honestly, people just don't know where models are headed and how they want to shape them yet and how they want humanity kind of like [inaudible 00:57:47] play a role in the future of all of this, and so I think there's a lot of opportunity to just continue shaping the discussion.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为有一个非常强大的生态系统，老实说，人们只是不知道模型的走向，以及他们想要如何塑造它们，以及他们希望人类如何[听不清 00:57:47] 在所有这一切的未来中发挥作用，所以我认为有很多机会继续塑造讨论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along that thread, I know you have a very strong thesis on just why this work matters to humanity and why this is so important, talk about that.
turns.zh: 沿着这条线索，我知道你有一个非常有力的论点，说明为什么这项工作对人类很重要，为什么它如此重要，请谈谈。

turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I'll get a bit philosophical here, but I think the question itself is a bit philosophical, so bear with me. So the most straightforward way of thinking about what we do is we train and evaluate AI. But there's a deeper mission that I often think about, which is helping our customers think about their dream objective functions. Like yeah, what kind of model do they want their model to be? And once we help them do that, we'll help them train their model to reach their north star and we'll help them measure that progress. But it's really hard because objective functions are really rich and complex. It's kind of like the difference between having a kid and asking them, "Okay, what test do you want to pass? Do you want them to get a high score on SAT and write a really good college essay?" That's a simplistic version versus what kind of person do you want them to grow up to be? Will you be happy if they're happy no matter what they do or are you hoping they'll go to a good school and be financially successful? (00:58:50): And again, if you take that notion, it's like, okay, how do you define happiness? How do you measure whether they're happy? How do you measure whether they're financially successful? It's a lot harder than something measuring whether or not you're getting a high score on the SAT, and what we're doing is we want to help our customers reach, again, their dream north stars and figure out how to measure them. And so I talked about this example of what you want models to do when you're asking them to write 50 different evaluations. Do you just continue them for 50 more or do you just say, "No, just move on [inaudible 00:59:25] because this is perfect enough." And the broader question is, are we building these systems that actually advance humanity? And if so how do we build the data sets to train towards that and measure it? Are we optimizing for all of these wrong things, just systems that suck up more and more of our time and make us lazier and lazier? (00:59:44): And yeah, I think it's really relevant to what we do because it's very hard and difficult to measure and define whether something is genuinely advancing humanity. It's very easy to measure all these proxies instead like clicks and likes. But I think that's why our work is so interesting. We want to work the hard, important metrics that require the hardest types of data and not just the easy ones. So I think one of the things I often say is you are your objective function. So we want the rich, complex, objective functions and not these simplistic proxies. And our job is to figure out how to get the data to match this. (01:00:12): So yeah, we want data, we want metrics that measure whether AI is making your life richer. We want to train our systems this way. And we want tools that make us more curious and more creative, not just lazier. And it's hard because, yeah, humans are kind of inherently lazy so AI software deals are the easiest way to get engagement, make all your metrics fall up. So I think this question about choosing the right objective functions and making sure that we're optimizing towards them and not just these easy proxies is really important to our future.
turns.zh: 我会在这里讲一点哲学，但我认为这个问题本身就有点哲学，所以请耐心听我说。因此，思考我们所做的事情最直接的方法是训练和评估人工智能。但我经常思考一个更深层次的使命，那就是帮助我们的客户思考他们梦想的目标函数。是的，他们希望自己的模特是什么样的？一旦我们帮助他们做到这一点，我们将帮助他们训练他们的模型以达到他们的北极星，我们将帮助他们衡量这一进展。但这确实很难，因为目标函数非常丰富且复杂。这有点像有一个孩子和问他们“好吧，你想通过什么考试？你希望他们在 SAT 考试中取得高分并写出一篇非常好的大学论文吗？”之间的区别。这是一个简单化的版本，而不是你希望他们长大成为什么样的人？如果他们无论做什么都快乐，或者你希望他们能上一所好学校并在经济上取得成功，你会感到高兴吗？ (00:58:50)：再说一次，如果你接受这个概念，那就像是，好吧，你如何定义幸福？你如何衡量他们是否快乐？您如何衡量他们在财务上是否成功？这比衡量你是否在 SAT 考试中获得高分要困难得多，而我们正在做的是，我们希望帮助我们的客户再次实现他们梦想的北极星，并弄清楚如何衡量它们。所以我谈到了这个例子，当你要求模型写出 50 种不同的评估时，你希望模型做什么。您是继续进行 50 次以上，还是只是说，“不，继续前进 [听不清 00:59:25]，因为这已经足够完美了。”更广泛的问题是，我们正在构建这些真正推动人类进步的系统吗？如果是这样，我们如何构建数据集来训练并测量它？我们是否正在针对所有这些错误的事情进行优化，只是那些占用我们越来越多时间并使我们变得越来越懒的系统？ (00:59:44)：是的，我认为这与我们所做的事情确实相关，因为衡量和定义某件事是否真正推动人类发展非常困难。衡量所有这些代理非常容易，例如点击次数和点赞次数。但我认为这就是我们的工作如此有趣的原因。我们希望研究需要最困难的数据类型的重要指标，而不仅仅是简单的数据。所以我认为我经常说的一件事是你就是你的目标函数。所以我们需要丰富、复杂的目标函数，而不是这些简单的代理。我们的工作是弄清楚如何获得与此相匹配的数据。 (01:00:12)：所以，是的，我们需要数据，我们需要衡量人工智能是否让你的生活变得更加丰富的指标。我们希望以这种方式训练我们的系统。我们需要工具让我们更加好奇、更加富有创造力，而不仅仅是更加懒惰。这很难，因为，是的，人类本质上是懒惰的，所以人工智能软件交易是获得参与度的最简单方法，让你的所有指标都下降。因此，我认为关于选择正确的目标函数并确保我们针对它们进行优化而不仅仅是这些简单的代理的问题对于我们的未来非常重要。

turns.en: Wow. I love how what you're sharing here gives you so much more appreciation of the nuances of building AI, training AI, the work that you're doing. (01:00:45): From the outside, people could just look at Surge and companies in the space of, okay, cool. They're just creating all this data, feeding it to AI. But clearly there's so much to this that people don't realize, and I love knowing that you're at the head of this, that someone like you is thinking through this so deeply. (01:01:02): Maybe one more question, is there something you wish you'd known before you started Surge? A lot of people start companies, they don't know what they're getting into. But I always thought that they were this magical ILR unicorn. So I thought if I started a company, I'd have to become a business person looking at financials all day and being in meetings all day and doing all this stuff that sounded incredibly boring and I always hated. And it's basically applied research where we're building all these amazing data systems that have really pushed the frontier of AI. turns.speaker: Edwin Chen
turns.en: I think the thing I would end with is I think a lot of people think of data labeling as it relates to simplistic work. Like labeling cat photos and drawing bounding box around cars. And so I've actually always hated the word data labeling because it just paints this very simplistic picture when I think what we're doing is completely different.
